title: The CPAT Mitigation Module: Methods in Brief
subtitle: How CPAT turns prices into fuel use, power investment, emissions and revenue
message: CPAT's mitigation module fits in about eighteen equations: a price identity, a two-margin demand equation, an engineering power model, emissions and revenue identities and a lagged GDP rule. A $50 carbon price cuts industrial coal by a third and road fuel by about 6 percent.

problem.text: CPAT covers more than 180 countries and informs carbon-tax and subsidy-reform advice. An economist who wants to know what it assumes had to assemble the method from tables, screenshots and equations that did not always match the spreadsheet.

mechanism.title: A one-way chain with lagged feedback
mechanism.caption: Blocks in calculation order; GDP and electricity prices feed back a year later.
points: Prices: supply cost plus taxes, less subsidies, plus the carbon charge and VAT on it.
Demand: income, usage and efficiency elasticities, all long-run.
Power: logit dispatch and investment; default cost of capital 7.5–15% by income group.
Revenue moves GDP a year later through multipliers.

action.title: Read CPAT as a first estimate
results: A $50/t price raises industrial coal 118% and cuts its use by 36%; road fuels fall about 6%.
No lags and almost no fuel switching outside power.
Road transport is described three times, and the three disagree.
